reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: The most commonly injured knee ligament, typically from a valgus force to the lateral knee
Graded I-III by the degree of medial laxity on valgus stress at 30 degrees of flexion
Pain and tenderness localise along the medial joint line and femoral or tibial attachment
The great majority of isolated MCL injuries heal without surgery owing to the ligament's good blood supply
Valgus laxity in full extension implies a more severe injury with cruciate or capsular involvement
Part of the 'unhappy triad' alongside ACL and medial meniscus injury
A Pellegrini-Stieda lesion (calcification at the femoral origin) can follow chronic proximal MCL injury
reference.pathophysiology: The superficial MCL is the primary restraint to valgus stress. A laterally directed blow or valgus load stretches or tears its fibres, most often at the femoral origin. Because the ligament is extra-articular with a rich blood supply, isolated tears typically heal with conservative management; combined injury to the cruciates or posteromedial corner produces greater instability and worse healing.
additionalDifferentials: Medial patellofemoral ligament injury after patellar dislocation
Physeal injury in skeletally immature patients
additionalInvestigations: Valgus stress testing at 0 and 30 degrees
MRI to grade the tear and detect associated injuries
Radiographs to exclude fracture and detect Pellegrini-Stieda calcification or physeal injury
Stress radiographs in skeletally immature patients to distinguish physeal fracture
redFlags: Valgus laxity in full extension indicating combined ligamentous injury
Physeal fracture mimicking ligament injury in children
reference.prognosis: Isolated MCL injuries of all grades usually recover well with bracing and rehabilitation; outcomes are less predictable when the injury is combined with cruciate or posteromedial corner damage.
pitfalls: Assuming an isolated MCL injury when valgus laxity in extension signals a combined injury
Missing a paediatric distal femoral physeal fracture that mimics MCL laxity
Overlooking a concurrent ACL or meniscal tear
Immobilising rigidly when early protected motion aids healing
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
